step1_summary: Chief complaint: Wheeze and shortness of breath for the past 2–3 days.

Symptoms: • Onset 2–3 days ago • Wheezing, exertional dyspnoea (unable to walk to work, sometimes cannot finish sentences) • Dry cough • Patient reports ‘fever’ but measured temperature 37 °C • No chest pain, no haemoptysis, no nocturnal symptoms, symptoms improve at rest.

Past medical history: Childhood asthma (severe enough to require occasional hospital visits), hay-fever, eczema. Asthma largely quiescent until recent flare; uses salbutamol PRN every few weeks and before exercise.
Medications/allergies: Salbutamol inhaler PRN; no regular meds; no drug allergies.
Social history: 33-year-old engineer, lives with partner, non-smoker, drinks ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days, normally walks to work but currently on sick leave/working from home due to dyspnoea.
Vital signs / exam: Tele-visit only. Reported temperature 37 °C (normal). No other vitals or physical-exam findings provided.

V: Pulmonary embolism: Acute onset dyspnoea; however wheeze is uncommon and no risk factors mentioned.
I: Viral upper/lower respiratory tract infection (incl. COVID-19) triggering asthma: Recent 2–3-day onset, mild fever, cough, wheeze.
Acute bronchitis: Cough and wheeze without sputum or high fever.
N: Endobronchial tumour (very unlikely given age, but could cause wheeze/obstruction).
D: Early-onset COPD / airway remodelling from longstanding asthma (asthma–COPD overlap) leading to baseline obstruction and easy exacerbations.
I2: Medication-induced bronchospasm (e.g., non-selective β-blocker) – no such drug reported but always consider iatrogenic causes.
C: Congenital airway abnormality (e.g., tracheomalacia) predisposing to wheeze—unlikely but fits congenital category.
A: Allergic asthma / pollen-induced exacerbation: Known atopy (hay fever, eczema); springtime pollen could trigger wheeze.
Acute allergic reaction (anaphylaxis spectrum) – less likely without urticaria, hypotension.
T: Airway irritation after inhalational exposure (smoke/fumes) – no exposure given, but trauma category includes environmental injury.
E: Thyrotoxicosis causing exertional dyspnoea/tachypnoea – no supporting evidence but metabolic causes considered.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation (likely triggered by viral infection or allergens)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: History of childhood and ongoing intermittent asthma, classic symptoms (wheeze, exertional dyspnoea, relief at rest), abrupt deterioration over 2–3 days, no alternative diagnosis more convincing.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral respiratory tract infection / acute bronchitis with reactive airway
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Short duration, mild ‘fever’, cough without sputum, could independently cause wheeze or precipitate asthma flare.
Atopic background (hay fever, eczema), springtime/allergen exposure often provokes asthma; no infectious signs other than patient-reported fever which was objectively normal.
Acute dyspnoea can resemble asthma, but wheeze uncommon; no chest pain, tachycardia or risk factors documented.
Cough and reported fever could suggest pneumonia, but normal temperature, absence of sputum, chest pain or focal findings argue against.

supporting_evidence: Previous diagnosis of asthma with inhaler use.
Classic symptoms: wheeze, shortness of breath, exertional limitation, occasional inability to finish sentences.
Known atopy (hay fever, eczema) – common comorbidity.
Good response plan given by physician (spacer, salbutamol) implies clinical impression matches asthma flare.
opposing_evidence: No nocturnal symptoms reported (typical in asthma).
Objective peak-flow or wheeze on exam not documented.

supporting_evidence: Dry cough without sputum common in early viral illness.
opposing_evidence: No rhinorrhoea, sore throat, myalgia or systemic viral symptoms documented.

supporting_evidence: History of hay fever and eczema (atopic triad).
Asthma commonly aggravated by seasonal allergens.
Symptoms predominantly respiratory with no infection signs.
opposing_evidence: Patient does not mention nasal/ocular allergy symptoms at this time.
Reports ‘fever’ (though normal), which is atypical for pure allergic reaction.
Age <40, no immobility, surgery, OCP, or thrombosis history.
Wheeze uncommon in PE; no pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, tachycardia, syncope.

supporting_evidence: Patient thought she had a fever.
Shortness of breath and cough can accompany pneumonia.
opposing_evidence: No productive sputum, chest pain, crackles/rales on exam, or systemic toxicity.
